title: Why Shareholder Rights Matter | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional argues shareholder rights are priced: stronger voting rights and disclosure lower perceived risk and discount rates, lifting valuations, so its stewardship votes against poison pills, staggered boards and dual-class structures. From July 2025 to June 2026 it backed 49 US proposals for annual director elections and voted against directors at 65 US companies that adopted poison pills without a shareholder vote. It also flags an SEC proposal that would drop certain disclosure requirements for about 81% of existing public companies, plus a May 2026 SEC proposal allowing semiannual rather than quarterly reporting.

themes.theme: Governance quality as a discount-rate input

insights.claim: Dimensional holds that shareholder rights are reflected in market prices: all else equal, stronger shareholder rights and more robust corporate governance reduce perceived risk and lower discount rates, producing higher valuations, while weaker rights raise discount rates and lower valuations.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Treat governance-rights deterioration (new pills, classified boards, super-voting shares, thinner disclosure) as a discount-rate shock, not a soft ESG factor; improvements are a potential re-rating catalyst.
insights.quote: stronger shareholder rights—and more robust corporate governance practices in general—can reduce perceived risk and lead to lower discount rates, resulting in higher valuations

insights.claim: Shareholder voting rights and company disclosures work together: without meaningful disclosure, shareholders cannot vote in an informed way, so weakening either one weakens the ability to hold boards and management accountable.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Assess governance risk on both axes together; a company with nominal voting rights but thin disclosure is still low-accountability.

insights.claim: Shareholder voting rights and disclosure quality vary widely across public companies, so shareholder rights are a company-specific characteristic rather than a uniform feature of public equity ownership.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Governance dispersion within an index is a source of cross-sectional valuation differences that can be screened for.

insights.claim: Dimensional generally votes against poison pills because, by limiting the market's ability to operate freely, they can block hostile takeovers that would have paid shareholders more than the company's current valuation, even when management has its own reasons to resist.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: A pill adoption caps takeover optionality and signals management entrenchment; expect large passive and factor holders to oppose it at the ballot.

insights.claim: In some markets, including the US, companies can adopt poison pills without a shareholder vote; when a portfolio company does so, Dimensional may vote against its directors both at that company and at every other portfolio company where those directors sit.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Unilateral pill adoption carries board-network consequences; expect lower director support votes across interlocked boards, which raises the reputational cost of entrenchment.
insights.quote: Dimensional may vote against directors at that company, as well as at any other portfolio company where those directors may serve

insights.claim: Between July 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026, Dimensional voted against directors at 65 US companies for adopting poison pills without shareholder approval and supported 49 management and shareholder proposals at US companies to adopt annual director elections.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Measures how often a major asset manager acts on its stewardship policy; unilateral pills remain common enough to prompt dozens of against-director votes each year.
insights.quote: voted against directors at 65 US companies for adopting poison pills without shareholder approval

insights.claim: Dimensional believes all directors should stand for reelection every year and views staggered or classified boards as poor governance because they shield directors from immediate accountability; it cites its research that shareholder value suffers when management and directors are not accountable.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Declassification proposals are likely to get institutional support; a classified board combined with a pill is a double entrenchment layer that justifies a governance discount.

insights.claim: Dimensional names voting against directors as one of the most important shareholder rights, because it is the main tool for holding directors accountable for actions that harm shareholders.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Watch withhold and against votes in director elections as the practical signal of institutional displeasure, more than the outcomes of precatory proposals.

insights.claim: Dimensional generally votes against management proposals that would limit shareholder rights and for proposals that would expand them, covering items such as share issuances and cumulative voting.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Management proposals that restrict rights face a structural 'no' vote from a large index-like holder; include this in proxy-outcome forecasts.

insights.claim: Dual-class structures, for example public Class A shares with one vote each and founder or insider Class B shares with 10 votes each, weaken ordinary shareholders' ability to hold boards accountable and to block value-harming actions such as poison pills; Dimensional generally supports proposals to remove unequal voting rights.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Public holders of super-voting-controlled companies have no real protection against entrenchment; price that governance risk in, especially for founder-led tech listings.
insights.locator: Why Shareholders Should Have Equal Voting Rights

insights.claim: According to the Council of Institutional Investors, about 9 in 10 US public companies have a single class of voting stock. Dimensional nonetheless concedes that academic evidence on whether dual-class shares raise or lower firm value is mixed.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Dual-class is a minority structure and its valuation penalty is not well established; opposition to it rests on governance principle more than on proven return drag.
insights.quote: The academic literature on whether the effect of dual-class shares on firm value is positive or negative is mixed.

insights.claim: As part of an effort to encourage companies to go public and stay public, the SEC has proposed amendments under which companies in their first five years as public companies, plus about 81% of all existing public companies, would no longer have to make certain disclosures.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Less mandated disclosure for most listed companies means more information asymmetry; by Dimensional's own logic that could raise discount rates, especially in smaller names that lose coverage.
insights.quote: approximately 81% of all existing public companies would no longer be required to make certain disclosures

insights.claim: In May 2026 the SEC proposed rules that would let public companies report semiannually instead of quarterly, a change Dimensional has researched in relation to financial reporting frequency and market premiums.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: A move to semiannual reporting would change the timing of earnings information and event-driven volatility; track which issuers opt out of quarterly reports.

insights.claim: Executive compensation plans are not uniform even within the same industry, so shareholders depend on company-specific disclosure to judge pay, yet companies with complex pay plans are not required to disclose more than those with simple plans, and often do not.
insights.speaker: Stephanie Hui
insights.so_what: Complex pay plans with thin disclosure are a governance warning flag, and would become harder to assess if the SEC cuts disclosure requirements.
insights.quote: it is not necessarily the case that a company with a complicated executive compensation plan will provide more extensive or detailed disclosures than a company with a simpler plan

source_meta.author: Stephanie Hui, Head of Responsible Investment and Senior Public Policy Strategist
